prerequisites: Knowledge and skills acquired in the Foundations of Computer Science course, including imperative programming, control structures, functions, basic abstract data types, and fundamental algorithmic concepts.
Ability to develop and understand simple programs, analyze their behavior, and apply basic principles of abstraction and modular design.

learning_outcomes.text: Describe the main data structures and algorithmic techniques presented in the course.
Explain the theoretical principles underlying correctness and complexity analysis.
Describe and analyze fundamental algorithms and properties of trees, heaps, hash tables, search trees, and graphs.
Distinguish advantages, limitations, and application domains of different algorithmic solutions.
Design algorithms for solving computational problems.
Select appropriate data structures according to application requirements.
Implement algorithms and data structures using object-oriented programming in Java.
Analyze correctness and efficiency through asymptotic analysis techniques.
Evaluate design choices in terms of correctness, efficiency, and maintainability.
Describe algorithms and data structures using appropriate technical terminology.
Justify and discuss design decisions clearly and rigorously.
Independently study new data structures and algorithmic techniques.
Use the acquired knowledge as a foundation for advanced courses.

syllabus_topics: Object-oriented programming in Java: classes, interfaces, inheritance, polymorphism, iterators.
Algorithm specification: computational models, computational problems, algorithms.
Algorithm analysis: combinatorial analysis, asymptotic analysis, induction, correctness and complexity analysis.
Trees: definitions, properties, traversals, binary trees.
Search trees: binary search trees and (2,4)-trees.
Graphs: definitions, properties, data structures for their representation, BFS, DFS, shortest paths, DAGs, and topological sorting.
Sorting algorithms and lower bounds for comparison-based sorting.
teaching_methods: Online formative quizzes with immediate feedback
Use of technological tools (Moodle, software, videos, quizzes, wooclap)

assessment_methods.method: Mandatory written exam - Part A (Theory and analysis)
Mandatory written exam - Part B (Algorithm design)
Possible oral examination (at the instructor’s discretion)

assessment_rules: The written exam is the primary assessment, lasting 150 minutes, and consists of two equally weighted parts (Part A: Theory and analysis, 16 points; Part B: Algorithm design, 16 points). Both parts must be individually sufficient to pass. Optional quizzes (up to 1 bonus point) and an optional individual programming project (up to 2 bonus points) can add to the written exam score if the written exam is passed. Bonus points are valid throughout the academic year and must be completed before the first examination session. Honours may be awarded if the overall score exceeds 31 points and outstanding mastery is demonstrated, at the instructor's discretion. The instructor may require an additional oral examination for clarification or better assessment.
